functions\\\",\\\"href\\\":\\\"https://supabase.com/docs/guides/troubleshooting/running-explain-analyze-on-functions\\\",\\\"content\\\":\\\"# Running EXPLAIN ANALYZE on functions\\\\n\\\\nSometimes it can help to look at Postgres query plans inside a function. The problem is that running [`EXPLAIN ANALYZE`](https://www.depesz.com/2013/04/16/explaining-the-unexplainable/) on a function usually just shows a [function scan](https://pganalyze.com/docs/explain/scan-nodes/function-scan) or result node, which gives little insight into how the queries actually perform.\\\\n\\\\n[`auto_explain`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/auto-explain.html) is a pre-installed module that is able to log query plans for queries within functions.\\\\n\\\\n`auto_explain` has a few settings that you still need to configure:\\\\n\\\\n* `auto_explain.log_nested_statements`: log the plans of queries within functions\\\\n* `auto_explain.log_analyze`: capture the `explain analyze` results instead of `explain`\\\\n* `auto_explain.log_min_duration`: if a query is expected to run for longer than the setting's threshold, log the plan\\\\n\\\\nChanging these settings at a broad scale can lead to excessive logging. Instead, you can change the configs within a `begin/rollback` block with the `set local` command. This ensures the changes are isolated to the transaction, and any writes made during testing are undone.\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\nbegin;\\\\n\\\\nset local auto_explain.log_min_duration = '0'; -- log all query plans\\\\nset local auto_explain.log_analyze = true; -- use explain analyze\\\\nset local auto_explain.log_buffers = true; -- use explain (buffers)\\\\nset local auto_explain.log_nested_statements = true; -- log query plans in functions\\\\n\\\\nselect example_func(); ---<--ADD YOUR FUNCTION HERE\\\\n\\\\nrollback;\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nIf needed, you can change these settings for specific roles, but we don't recommend configuring the value below `1s` for extended periods, as it may degrade performance.\\\\n\\\\nFor instance, you could change the value for the authenticator role (powers the Data API).\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\nALTER ROLE postgres SET auto_explain.log_min_duration = '.5s';\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nAfter running your test, you should be able to find the plan in the [Postgres logs](/dashboard/project/_/logs/postgres-logs?s=duration:). The auto\\\\\\\\_explain module always starts logs with the term \\\\\\\"duration:\\\\\\\", which can be used as a filter keyword.\\\\n\\\\nYou can also filter for the specific function in the [log explorer](/dashboard/project/_/logs/explorer?q=select%0A++cast%28postgres_logs.timestamp+as+datetime%29+as+timestamp%2C%0A++event_message+AS+query_and_plan%2C%0A++parsed.user_name%2C%0A++parsed.context%0Afrom%0A++postgres_logs%0A++cross+join+unnest%28metadata%29+as+metadata%0A++cross+join+unnest%28metadata.parsed%29+as+parsed%0Awhere%0A++regexp_contains%28event_message%2C+%27duration%3A%27%29%0A++AND%0A++regexp_contains%28context%2C+%27example_func%27%29+--%3C----ADD+FUNCTION+NAME+HERE.+IS+CASE+SENSITIVE%0Aorder+by+timestamp+desc%0Alimit+100%3B) with the below query:\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\nselect\\\\n cast(postgres_logs.timestamp as datetime) as timestamp,\\\\n event_message as query_and_plan,\\\\n parsed.user_name,\\\\n parsed.context\\\\nfrom\\\\n postgres_logs\\\\n cross join unnest(metadata) as metadata\\\\n cross join unnest(metadata.parsed) as parsed\\\\nwhere regexp_contains(event_message, 'duration:') and regexp_contains(context, '(?i)FUNCTION_NAME')\\\\norder by timestamp desc\\\\nlimit 100;\\\\n```\\\\n\\\"},{\\\"title\\\":\\\"RLS Performance and Best Practices\\\",\\\"href\\\":\\\"https://supabase.com/docs/guides/troubleshooting/rls-performance-and-best-practices-Z5Jjwv\\\",\\\"content\\\":\\\"# RLS Performance and Best Practices\\\\n\\\\n## RLS performance and best practices\\\\n\\\\nAlthough most of the time spent on thinking about RLS is to get it to handle security needs, the impact of it on performance of your queries can be massive.\\\\nThis is especially true on queries that look at every row in a table like for many select operations and updates.\\\\nNote that queries that use limit and offset will usually have to query all rows to determine order, not just the limit amount so they are impacted too.\\\\n\\\\nSee the last section for ways to measure the performance of your queries as you test RLS improvements.\\\\n\\\\n### Is RLS causing performance issues (on a single table query)?\\\\n\\\\nFor very slow queries, or if using the tools at end of article, run a query with RLS enabled on the table and then with it disabled (this should only be done in a non production environment). If the results are similar then your query itself is likely the performance issue. Although, remember any join tables in RLS will also need to run their RLS unless a security definer function is used to bypass them. You can also create a service\\\\\\\\_role client to run the query bypassing RLS if in a secure environment.\\\\n\\\\n### How to improve RLS performance.\\\\n\\\\nThe following tips are very broad and each may or may not help the specific case involved. Some changes, like adding indexes, should be backed out if they do not make a difference in RLS performance and you are not using them for filtering performance.\\\\n\\\\n#### 1. The first thing to try is put an index on columns used in the RLS that are not primary keys or unique already.\\\\n\\\\nFor RLS like:\\\\n`auth.uid() = user_id`\\\\nAdd an index like:\\\\n`create index userid on test_table using btree (user_id) tablespace pg_default;`\\\\nImprovement seen over 100x on large tables.\\\\n\\\\n#### 2. Another method to improve performance is to wrap your RLS queries and functions in select statements.\\\\n\\\\nThis method works well for JWT functions like `auth.uid()` and `auth.jwt()` as well as any other functions including security definer type.\\\\nWrapping the function in some SQL causes an `initPlan` to be run by the optimizer which allows it to \\\\\\\"cache\\\\\\\" the results versus calling the function\\\\non each row.\\\\nWARNING: You can only do this if the results of the query or function do not change based on the row data.\\\\nFor RLS like this:\\\\n`is_admin() or auth.uid() = user_id`\\\\nUse this instead:\\\\n`(select is_admin()) OR (select auth.uid()) = user_id`\\\\n\\\\n#### 3. Do not rely on RLS for filtering but only for security.\\\\n\\\\nInstead of doing this (JS client example):\\\\n`.from('table').select()`\\\\nWith an RLS policy of:\\\\n`auth.uid() = user_id`\\\\nAdd a filter in addition to the RLS:\\\\n`.from('table').select().eq('user_id',userId)`\\\\n\\\\n#### 4. Use security definer functions to do queries on other tables to bypass their RLS when possible.\\\\n\\\\nInstead of having this RLS where the roles\\\\\\\\_table has an RLS select policy of `auth.uid() = user_id`:\\\\n`exists (select 1 from roles_table where auth.uid() = user_id and role = 'good_role')`\\\\nCreate a security definer function has\\\\\\\\_role() and do:\\\\n`(select has_role())` with code of `exists (select 1 from roles_table where auth.uid() = user_id and role = 'good_role')`\\\\nNote that you should wrap your security definer function in select if it is a fixed value per 2.\\\\nRemember functions you use in RLS can be called from the API.\\\\nSecure your functions in an alternate schema if their results would be a security leak.\\\\nWarning: If your security definer function uses row information as an input parameter be sure to test performance as you can't wrap the function as in 2.\\\\n\\\\n#### 5. Always optimize join queries to compare row columns to fixed join data.\\\\n\\\\nInstead of querying on a row column in a join table WHERE, organize your query to get all\\\\nthe column values that meet your query into an array or set.\\\\nThen use an IN or ANY operation to filter against the row column.\\\\nThis RLS to allow select only for rows where the team\\\\\\\\_id is one the user has access to:\\\\n`auth.uid() in (select user_id from team_user where team_user.team_id = table.team_id)`\\\\nwill be much slower than:\\\\n`team_id in (select team_id from team_user where user_id = auth.uid())`\\\\nAlso consider moving the join query to a security definer function to avoid RLS on join table:\\\\n`team_id in (select user_teams())`\\\\nNote that if the `in` list gets to be over 10K items, then extra analysis is likely needed. See this follow up testing: .\\\\n\\\\n#### 6. Use role in TO option or roles dropdown in the dashboard.\\\\n\\\\nNever just use RLS involving `auth.uid()` or `auth.jwt()` as your way to rule out 'anon' role.\\\\nAlways add 'authenticated' to the approved roles instead of nothing or public.\\\\nAlthough this does not improve the query performance for the signed in user it does\\\\neliminate 'anon' users without taxing the database to process the rest of the RLS.\\\\n\\\\n### Sample results\\\\n\\\\nThe code used for the below tests can be found here: [LINK](https://github.com/GaryAustin1/RLS-Perfomance):\\\\nThe tests are doing selects on a 100K row table. Some have an additional join table.\\\\n\\\\nShow RLS and before after for above examples.\\\\n\\\\n| Test | RLS Before | RLS After | SQL | SQL |\\\\n| ---- | ---------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | ------- | --- |\\\\n| 1 | auth.uid()=user\\\\\\\\_id | user\\\\\\\\_id indexed | 171ms | <.1 |\\\\n| 2a | auth.uid()=user\\\\\\\\_id | (select auth.uid()) = user\\\\\\\\_id | 179 | 9 |\\\\n| 2b | is*admin() \\\\\\\\_table join* | (select is*admin()) \\\\\\\\_table join* | 11,000 | 7 |\\\\n| 2c | is\\\\\\\\_admin() OR auth.uid()=user\\\\\\\\_id | (select is\\\\\\\\_admin()) OR (select auth.uid()=user\\\\\\\\_id) | 11,000 | 10 |\\\\n| 2d | has\\\\\\\\_role()=role | (select has\\\\\\\\_role())=role | 178,000 | 12 |\\\\n| 2e | team\\\\\\\\_id=any(user\\\\\\\\_teams()) | team\\\\\\\\_id=any(array(select user\\\\\\\\_teams())) | 173000 | 16 |\\\\n| 3 | auth.uid()=user\\\\\\\\_id | add .eq or where on user\\\\\\\\_id | 171 | 9 |\\\\n| 5 | auth.uid() in *table join on col* | col in *table join on auth.uid()* | 9,000 | 20 |\\\\n| 6 | No TO policy | TO authenticated (anon accessing) | 170 | <.1 |\\\\n\\\\n### Tools to measure performance\\\\n\\\\nPostgres has tools to analyze the performance of queries. \\\\nThe use of explain in detail for query analysis is beyond the scope of this discussion.\\\\nHere we will use it mainly to get a performance metric to compare times.\\\\nIn order to do RLS testing you need to setup the user JWT claims and change the running user to `anon` or `authenticated`.\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\nset session role authenticated;\\\\nset request.jwt.claims to '{\\\\\\\"role\\\\\\\":\\\\\\\"authenticated\\\\\\\", \\\\\\\"sub\\\\\\\":\\\\\\\"5950b438-b07c-4012-8190-6ce79e4bd8e5\\\\\\\"}';\\\\n\\\\nexplain analyze SELECT count(*) FROM rlstest;\\\\nset session role postgres;\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nThis will return results like:\\\\n\\\\n Seq Scan on rlstest (cost=0.00..4334.00 rows=1 width=35) (actual time=170.999..170.999 rows=0 loops=1)\\\\n \\\\\\\" Filter: ((COALESCE(NULLIF(current_setting('request.jwt.claim.sub'::text, true), ''::text), ((NULLIF(current_setting('request.jwt.claims'::text, true), ''::text))::jsonb ->> 'sub'::text)))::uuid = user_id)\\\\\\\"\\\\n Rows Removed by Filter: 100000\\\\n Planning Time: 0.216 ms\\\\n Execution Time: 171.033 ms\\\\n\\\\nIn this case the execution time is the critical number we need to compare.\\\\n\\\\nPostgREST allows use of explain to get performance information on your queries with Supabase clients.\\\\n\\\\nBefore using this feature you need to run the following command in the Dashboard SQL editor (should not be used in production):\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\nalter role authenticator set pgrst.db_plan_enabled to true;\\\\nNOTIFY pgrst, 'reload config';\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nThen you can use the .explain() modifier to get performance metrics.\\\\n\\\\n```js\\\\nconst { data, error } = await supabase\\\\n .from('projects')\\\\n .select('*')\\\\n .eq('id', 1)\\\\n .explain({ analyze: true })\\\\n\\\\nconsole.log(data)\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nThis will return a result like:\\\\n\\\\n Aggregate (cost=8.18..8.20 rows=1 width=112) (actual time=0.017..0.018 rows=1 loops=1)\\\\n -> Index Scan using projects_pkey on projects (cost=0.15..8.17 rows=1 width=40) (actual time=0.012..0.012 rows=0 loops=1)\\\\n Index Cond: (id = 1)\\\\n Filter: false\\\\n Rows Removed by Filter: 1\\\\n Planning Time: 0.092 ms\\\\n Execution Time: 0.046 ms\\\\n\\\\n\\\\\\\\*These two GitHub discussions cover the history that lead to this analysis...\\\\n\\\\n[Stable functions do not seem to be honored in RLS in basic form](https://github.com/orgs/supabase/discussions/9311)\\\\n[current\\\\\\\\_setting can lead to bad performance when used on RLS](https://github.com/PostgREST/postgrest-docs/issues/609#)\\\\n\\\\nThanks Steve Chavez and Wolfgang Walther in those threads.\\\\n\\\\n### Added example of security definer function having select of a team table, comparing against a column in main table\\\\n\\\\nThe example is in the test data as test2f.\\\\nIn this case we start with a 1M row table with a team\\\\\\\\_id column.\\\\nWe have a 1000 row team table that has user\\\\\\\\_ids and team(s) they belong too.\\\\nBasic RLS for a select would be `team_id = ANY(user_teams())`\\\\nThis case times out with over 3 minutes as 1M rows must be searched and the function is run each time on 1000 rows.\\\\nChanging to wrap the function (method 2) `team_id = ANY(ARRAY(select user_teams()))` is a big improvement but can still take seconds.\\\\nAdding an index to team\\\\\\\\_id is the big win, but only with the second case. Without, the index case still times out.\\\\n\\\\nSome results:\\\\n\\\\n| Policy | Index | Main Rs | Team Rs | on 10 teams | 100 | 500 | note |\\\\n| --------------------------------- | ----- | ------- | ------- | ----------- | ----- | ----- | ------------------ |\\\\n| =ANY(user\\\\\\\\_teams()) | no | 1M | 1000 | >2Min | >2Min | >2Min | TO or killed |\\\\n| =ANY(user\\\\\\\\_teams()) | yes | 1M | 1000 | >2Min | >2Min | >2Min | TO or killed |\\\\n| =ANY(ARRAY(select user\\\\\\\\_teams())) | no | 1M | 1000 | 170ms | 700 | 3300 | |\\\\n| =ANY(ARRAY(select user\\\\\\\\_teams())) | yes | 1M | 1000 | 2ms | 3 | 3 | |\\\\n| in(1,2,3...100) | no | 1M | NA | 130ms | 142 | x | baseline check |\\\\n| =ANY(ARRAY(select user\\\\\\\\_teams())) | yes | 1M | 10K | x | x | x | 24ms (on 1K teams) |\\\\n\\\"},{\\\"title\\\":\\\"HypoPG: Hypothetical indexes\\\",\\\"href\\\":\\\"https://supabase.com/docs/guides/database/extensions/hypopg\\\",\\\"content\\\":\\\"# HypoPG: Hypothetical indexes\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n`HypoPG` is Postgres extension for creating hypothetical/virtual indexes. HypoPG allows users to rapidly create hypothetical/virtual indexes that have no resource cost (CPU, disk, memory) that are visible to the Postgres query planner.\\\\n\\\\nThe motivation for HypoPG is to allow users to quickly search for an index to improve a slow query without consuming server resources or waiting for them to build.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Enable the extension\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n \\\\n 1. Go to the [Database](/dashboard/project/_/database/tables) page in the Dashboard.\\\\n 2. Click on **Extensions** in the sidebar.\\\\n 3. Search for `hypopg` and enable the extension.\\\\n \\\\n\\\\n \\\\n {/* prettier-ignore */}\\\\n\\\\n ```sql\\\\n -- Enable the \\\\\\\"hypopg\\\\\\\" extension\\\\n create extension hypopg with schema extensions;\\\\n\\\\n -- Disable the \\\\\\\"hypopg\\\\\\\" extension\\\\n drop extension if exists hypopg;\\\\n ```\\\\n\\\\n Even though the SQL code is `create extension`, this is the equivalent of enabling the extension.\\\\n To disable an extension you can call `drop extension`.\\\\n\\\\n It's good practice to create the extension within a separate schema (like `extensions`) to keep the `public` schema clean.\\\\n \\\\n\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Speeding up a query\\\\n\\\\nGiven the following table and a simple query to select from the table by `id`:\\\\n\\\\n{/* prettier-ignore */}\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\ncreate table account (\\\\n id int,\\\\n address text\\\\n);\\\\n\\\\ninsert into account(id, address)\\\\nselect\\\\n id,\\\\n id || ' main street'\\\\nfrom\\\\n generate_series(1, 10000) id;\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nWe can generate an explain plan for a description of how the Postgres query planner\\\\nintends to execute the query.\\\\n\\\\n{/* prettier-ignore */}\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\nexplain select * from account where id=1;\\\\n\\\\n QUERY PLAN\\\\n-------------------------------------------------------\\\\n Seq Scan on account (cost=0.00..180.00 rows=1 width=13)\\\\n Filter: (id = 1)\\\\n(2 rows)\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nUsing HypoPG, we can create a hypothetical index on the `account(id)` column to check if it would be useful to the query planner and then re-run the explain plan.\\\\n\\\\nNote that the virtual indexes created by HypoPG are only visible in the Postgres connection that they were created in. Supabase connects to Postgres through a connection pooler so the `hypopg_create_index` statement and the `explain` statement should be executed in a single query.\\\\n\\\\n{/* prettier-ignore */}\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\nselect * from hypopg_create_index('create index on account(id)');\\\\n\\\\nexplain select * from account where id=1;\\\\n\\\\n QUERY PLAN\\\\n------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\\\\n Index Scan using <13504>btree_account_id on hypo (cost=0.29..8.30 rows=1 width=13)\\\\n Index Cond: (id = 1)\\\\n(2 rows)\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nThe query plan has changed from a `Seq Scan` to an `Index Scan` using the newly created virtual index, so we may choose to create a real version of the index to improve performance on the target query:\\\\n\\\\n{/* prettier-ignore */}\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\ncreate index on account(id);\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Functions\\\\n\\\\n* [`hypo_create_index(text)`](https://hypopg.readthedocs.io/en/rel1_stable/usage.html#create-a-hypothetical-index): A function to create a hypothetical index.\\\\n* [`hypopg_list_indexes`](https://hypopg.readthedocs.io/en/rel1_stable/usage.html#manipulate-hypothetical-indexes): A View that lists all hypothetical indexes that have been created.\\\\n* [`hypopg()`](https://hypopg.readthedocs.io/en/rel1_stable/usage.html#manipulate-hypothetical-indexes): A function that lists all hypothetical indexes that have been created with the same format as `pg_index`.\\\\n* [`hypopg_get_index_def(oid)`](https://hypopg.readthedocs.io/en/rel1_stable/usage.html#manipulate-hypothetical-indexes): A function to display the `create index` statement that would create the index.\\\\n* [`hypopg_get_relation_size(oid)`](https://hypopg.readthedocs.io/en/rel1_stable/usage.html#manipulate-hypothetical-indexes): A function to estimate how large a hypothetical index would be.\\\\n* [`hypopg_drop_index(oid)`](https://hypopg.readthedocs.io/en/rel1_stable/usage.html#manipulate-hypothetical-indexes): A function to remove a given hypothetical index by `oid`.\\\\n* [`hypopg_reset()`](https://hypopg.readthedocs.io/en/rel1_stable/usage.html#manipulate-hypothetical-indexes): A function to remove all hypothetical indexes.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Resources\\\\n\\\\n* Official [HypoPG documentation](https://hypopg.readthedocs.io/en/rel1_stable/)\\\\n\\\"},{\\\"title\\\":\\\"Debugging performance issues\\\",\\\"href\\\":\\\"https://supabase.com/docs/guides/database/debugging-performance\\\",\\\"content\\\":\\\"# Debugging performance issues\\\\n\\\\nDebug slow-running queries using the Postgres execution planner.\\\\n\\\\n`explain()` is a method that provides the Postgres `EXPLAIN` execution plan of a query. It is a powerful tool for debugging slow queries and understanding how Postgres will execute a given query. This feature is applicable to any query, including those made through `rpc()` or write operations.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Enabling `explain()`\\\\n\\\\n`explain()` is disabled by default to protect sensitive information about your database structure and operations. We recommend using `explain()` in a non-production environment. Run the following SQL to enable `explain()`:\\\\n\\\\n{/* prettier-ignore */}\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\n-- enable explain\\\\nalter role authenticator\\\\nset pgrst.db_plan_enabled to 'true';\\\\n\\\\n-- reload the config\\\\nnotify pgrst, 'reload config';\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Using `explain()`\\\\n\\\\nTo get the execution plan of a query, you can chain the `explain()` method to a Supabase query:\\\\n\\\\n{/* prettier-ignore */}\\\\n\\\\n```ts\\\\nconst { data, error } = await supabase\\\\n .from('instruments')\\\\n .select()\\\\n .explain()\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Example data\\\\n\\\\nTo illustrate, consider the following setup of a `instruments` table:\\\\n\\\\n{/* prettier-ignore */}\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\ncreate table instruments (\\\\n id int8 primary key,\\\\n name text\\\\n);\\\\n\\\\ninsert into books\\\\n (id, name)\\\\nvalues\\\\n (1, 'violin'),\\\\n (2, 'viola'),\\\\n (3, 'cello');\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Expected response\\\\n\\\\nThe response would typically look like this:\\\\n\\\\n{/* prettier-ignore */}\\\\n\\\\n```markdown\\\\nAggregate (cost=33.34..33.36 rows=1 width=112)\\\\n -> Limit (cost=0.00..18.33 rows=1000 width=40)\\\\n -> Seq Scan on instruments (cost=0.00..22.00 rows=1200 width=40)\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nBy default, the execution plan is returned in TEXT format. However, you can also retrieve it as JSON by specifying the `format` parameter.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Production use with pre-request protection\\\\n\\\\nIf you need to enable `explain()` in a production environment, ensure you protect your database by restricting access to the `explain()` feature. You can do so by using a pre-request function that filters requests based on the IP address:\\\\n\\\\n{/* prettier-ignore */}\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\ncreate or replace function filter_plan_requests()\\\\nreturns void as $$\\\\ndeclare\\\\n headers json := current_setting('request.headers', true)::json;\\\\n client_ip text := coalesce(headers->>'cf-connecting-ip', '');\\\\n accept text := coalesce(headers->>'accept', '');\\\\n your_ip text := '123.123.123.123'; -- replace this with your IP\\\\nbegin\\\\n if accept like 'application/vnd.pgrst.plan%' and client_ip != your_ip then\\\\n raise insufficient_privilege using\\\\n message = 'Not allowed to use application/vnd.pgrst.plan';\\\\n end if;\\\\nend; $$ language plpgsql;\\\\nalter role authenticator set pgrst.db_pre_request to 'filter_plan_requests';\\\\nnotify pgrst, 'reload config';\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n The `pgrst.db_pre_request` configuration only works with the **Data API** (PostgREST). It does not work with Realtime, Storage, or other Supabase products.\\\\n\\\\n If you're using `db_pre_request` to call a function (like `set_information()`) that sets up context or performs checks on every request, and you need similar behavior for other Supabase products, you must call the function directly in your Row Level Security (RLS) policies instead.\\\\n\\\\n **Example:**\\\\n\\\\n If you have a `db_pre_request` function that calls `set_information()` that returns `true` to set up context or perform checks, and you have an RLS policy like:\\\\n\\\\n ```sql\\\\n create policy \\\\\\\"Individuals can view their own todos.\\\\\\\"\\\\n on todos for select\\\\n using ( (select auth.uid()) = user_id );\\\\n ```\\\\n\\\\n To achieve the same behavior with other Supabase products, you need to call the function directly in your RLS policy:\\\\n\\\\n ```sql\\\\n create policy \\\\\\\"Individuals can view their own todos.\\\\\\\"\\\\n on todos for select\\\\n using ( set_information() AND (select auth.uid()) = user_id );\\\\n ```\\\\n\\\\n This ensures the function is called when evaluating RLS policies for all products, not just Data API requests.\\\\n\\\\n **Performance consideration:**\\\\n\\\\n Be aware that calling functions directly in RLS policies can impact database performance, as the function is evaluated for each row when the policy is checked. Consider optimizing your function or using caching strategies if performance becomes an issue.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\nReplace `'123.123.123.123'` with your actual IP address.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Disabling explain\\\\n\\\\nTo disable the `explain()` method after use, execute the following SQL commands:\\\\n\\\\n{/* prettier-ignore */}\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\n-- disable explain\\\\nalter role authenticator\\\\nset pgrst.db_plan_enabled to 'false';\\\\n\\\\n-- if you used the above pre-request\\\\nalter role authenticator\\\\nset pgrst.db_pre_request to '';\\\\n\\\\n-- reload the config\\\\nnotify pgrst, 'reload config';\\\\n```\\\\n\\\"},{\\\"title\\\":\\\"Managing Indexes in PostgreSQL\\\",\\\"href\\\":\\\"https://supabase.com/docs/guides/database/postgres/indexes\\\",\\\"content\\\":\\\"# Managing Indexes in PostgreSQL\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n\\\\nAn index makes your Postgres queries faster. The index is like a \\\\\\\"table of contents\\\\\\\" for your data - a reference list which allows queries to quickly locate a row in a given table without needing to scan the entire table (which in large tables can take a long time).\\\\n\\\\nIndexes can be structured in a few different ways. The type of index chosen depends on the values you are indexing. By far the most common index type, and the default in Postgres, is the B-Tree. A B-Tree is the generalized form of a binary search tree, where nodes can have more than two children.\\\\n\\\\nEven though indexes improve query performance, the Postgres query planner may not always make use of a given index when choosing which optimizations to make. Additionally indexes come with some overhead - additional writes and increased storage - so it's useful to understand how and when to use indexes, if at all.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Create an index\\\\n\\\\nLet's take an example table:\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\ncreate table persons (\\\\n id bigint generated by default as identity primary key,\\\\n age int,\\\\n height int,\\\\n weight int,\\\\n name text,\\\\n deceased boolean\\\\n);\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n All the queries in this guide can be run using the [SQL Editor](/dashboard/project/_/sql) in the Supabase Dashboard, or via `psql` if you're [connecting directly to the database](/docs/guides/database/connecting-to-postgres#direct-connections).\\\\n\\\\n\\\\nWe might want to frequently query users based on their age:\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\nselect name from persons where age = 32;\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nWithout an index, Postgres will scan every row in the table to find equality matches on age.\\\\n\\\\nYou can verify this by doing an explain on the query:\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\nexplain select name from persons where age = 32;\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nOutputs:\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nSeq Scan on persons (cost=0.00..22.75 rows=x width=y)\\\\nFilter: (age = 32)\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nTo add a simple B-Tree index you can run:\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\ncreate index idx_persons_age on persons (age);\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n It can take a long time to build indexes on large datasets and the default behaviour of `create index` is to lock the table from writes.\\\\n\\\\n Luckily Postgres provides us with `create index concurrently` which prevents blocking writes on the table, but does take a bit longer to build.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\nHere is a simplified diagram of the index we just created (note that in practice, nodes actually have more than two children).\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n\\\\nYou can see that in any large data set, traversing the index to locate a given value can be done in much less operations (O(log n)) than compared to scanning the table one value at a time from top to bottom (O(n)).\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Partial indexes\\\\n\\\\nIf you are frequently querying a subset of rows then it may be more efficient to build a partial index. In our example, perhaps we only want to match on `age` where `deceased is false`. We could build a partial index:\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\ncreate index idx_living_persons_age on persons (age)\\\\nwhere deceased is false;\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Ordering indexes\\\\n\\\\nBy default B-Tree indexes are sorted in ascending order, but sometimes you may want to provide a different ordering. Perhaps our application has a page featuring the top 10 oldest people. Here we would want to sort in descending order, and include `NULL` values last. For this we can use:\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\ncreate index idx_persons_age_desc on persons (age desc nulls last);\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Reindexing\\\\n\\\\nAfter a while indexes can become stale and may need rebuilding. Postgres provides a `reindex` command for this, but due to Postgres locks being placed on the index during this process, you may want to make use of the `concurrent` keyword.\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\nreindex index concurrently idx_persons_age;\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nAlternatively you can reindex all indexes on a particular table:\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\nreindex table concurrently persons;\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nTake note that `reindex` can be used inside a transaction, but `reindex [index/table] concurrently` cannot.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Index Advisor\\\\n\\\\nIndexes can improve query performance of your tables as they grow. The Supabase Dashboard offers an Index Advisor, which suggests potential indexes to add to your tables.\\\\n\\\\nFor more information on the Index Advisor and its suggestions, see the [`index_advisor` extension](/docs/guides/database/extensions/index_advisor).\\\\n\\\\nTo use the Dashboard Index Advisor:\\\\n\\\\n1. Go to the [Query Performance](/dashboard/project/_/advisors/query-performance) page.\\\\n2. Click on a query to bring up the Details side panel.\\\\n3. Select the Indexes tab.\\\\n4. Enable Index Advisor if prompted.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Understanding Index Advisor results\\\\n\\\\nThe Indexes tab shows the existing indexes used in the selected query. Note that indexes suggested in the \\\\\\\"New Index Recommendations\\\\\\\" section may not be used when you create them. Postgres' query planner may intentionally ignore an available index if it determines that the query will be faster without. For example, on a small table, a sequential scan might be faster than an index scan. In that case, the planner will switch to using the index as the table size grows, helping to future proof the query.\\\\n\\\\nIf additional indexes might improve your query, the Index Advisor shows the suggested indexes with the estimated improvement in startup and total costs:\\\\n\\\\n* Startup cost is the cost to fetch the first row\\\\n* Total cost is the cost to fetch all the rows\\\\n\\\\nCosts are in arbitrary units, where a single sequential page read costs 1.0 units.\\\\n\\\"},{\\\"title\\\":\\\"Using Explain\\\",\\\"href\\\":\\\"https://supabase.com/docs/reference/swift/explain\\\",\\\"content\\\":\\\"# Swift Reference\\\\n\\\\nUsing Explain\\\\n\\\\nFor debugging slow queries, you can get the [Postgres `EXPLAIN` execution plan](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-explain.html) of a query\\\\nusing the `explain()` method. This works on any query, even for `rpc()` or writes.\\\\n\\\\nExplain is not enabled by default as it can reveal sensitive information about your database.\\\\nIt's best to only enable this for testing environments but if you wish to enable it for production you can provide additional protection by using a `pre-request` function.\\\\n\\\\nFollow the [Performance Debugging Guide](/docs/guides/database/debugging-performance) to enable the functionality on your project.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Examples\\\\n\\\\n### Get the execution plan\\\\n\\\\n```swift\\\\ntry await supabase\\\\n .from(\\\\\\\"instruments\\\\\\\")\\\\n .select()\\\\n .explain()\\\\n .execute()\\\\n .value\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Get the execution plan with analyze and verbose\\\\n\\\\n```swift\\\\ntry await supabase\\\\n .from(\\\\\\\"instruments\\\\\\\")\\\\n .select()\\\\n .explain(\\\\n analyze: true,\\\\n verbose: true\\\\n )\\\\n .execute()\\\\n .value\\\\n```\\\\n\\\"},{\\\"title\\\":\\\"Database configuration\\\",\\\"href\\\":\\\"https://supabase.com/docs/guides/database/postgres/configuration\\\",\\\"content\\\":\\\"# Database configuration\\\\n\\\\nUpdating the default configuration for your Postgres database.\\\\n\\\\nPostgres provides a set of sensible defaults for you database size. In some cases, these defaults can be updated. We do not recommend changing these defaults unless you know what you're doing.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Timeouts\\\\n\\\\nSee the [Timeouts](/docs/guides/database/postgres/timeouts) section.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Statement optimization\\\\n\\\\nAll Supabase projects come with the [`pg_stat_statements`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/pgstatstatements.html) extension installed, which tracks planning and execution statistics for all statements executed against it. These statistics can be used in order to diagnose the performance of your project.\\\\n\\\\nThis data can further be used in conjunction with the [`explain`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/using-explain.html) functionality of Postgres to optimize your usage.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Managing timezones\\\\n\\\\nEvery Supabase database is set to UTC timezone by default. We strongly recommend keeping it this way, even if your users are in a different location. This is because it makes it much easier to calculate differences between timezones if you adopt the mental model that everything in your database is in UTC time.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Change timezone\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n \\\\n ```sql\\\\n alter database postgres\\\\n set timezone to 'America/New_York';\\\\n ```\\\\n \\\\n\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Full list of timezones\\\\n\\\\nGet a full list of timezones supported by your database. This will return the following columns:\\\\n\\\\n* `name`: Time zone name\\\\n* `abbrev`: Time zone abbreviation\\\\n* `utc_offset`: Offset from UTC (positive means east of Greenwich)\\\\n* `is_dst`: True if currently observing daylight savings\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n \\\\n ```sql\\\\n select name, abbrev, utc_offset, is_dst\\\\n from pg_timezone_names()\\\\n order by name;\\\\n ```\\\\n \\\\n\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Search for a specific timezone\\\\n\\\\nUse `ilike` (case insensitive search) to find specific timezones.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n \\\\n ```sql\\\\n select *\\\\n from pg_timezone_names()\\\\n where name ilike '%york%';\\\\n ```\\\\n \\\\n\\\\n\\\"},{\\\"title\\\":\\\"Using Explain\\\",\\\"href\\\":\\\"https://supabase.com/docs/reference/python/explain\\\",\\\"content\\\":\\\"# Python Reference\\\\n\\\\nUsing Explain\\\\n\\\\nFor debugging slow queries, you can get the [Postgres `EXPLAIN` execution plan](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-explain.html) of a query\\\\nusing the `explain()` method. This works on any query, even for `rpc()` or writes.\\\\n\\\\nExplain is not enabled by default as it can reveal sensitive information about your database.\\\\nIt's best to only enable this for testing environments but if you wish to enable it for production you can provide additional protection by using a `pre-request` function.\\\\n\\\\nFollow the [Performance Debugging Guide](/docs/guides/database/debugging-performance) to enable the functionality on your project.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Examples\\\\n\\\\n### Get the execution plan\\\\n\\\\n```python\\\\nresponse = (\\\\n supabase.table(\\\\\\\"planets\\\\\\\")\\\\n .select(\\\\\\\"*\\\\\\\")\\\\n .explain()\\\\n .execute()\\\\n)\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Get the execution plan with analyze and verbose\\\\n\\\\n```python\\\\nresponse = (\\\\n supabase.table(\\\\\\\"planets\\\\\\\")\\\\n .select(\\\\\\\"*\\\\\\\")\\\\n .explain(analyze=True, verbose=True)\\\\n .execute()\\\\n)\\\\n```\\\\n\\\"},{\\\"title\\\":\\\"Using Explain\\\",\\\"href\\\":\\\"https://supabase.com/docs/reference/dart/explain\\\",\\\"content\\\":\\\"# Dart Reference\\\\n\\\\nUsing Explain\\\\n\\\\nFor debugging slow queries, you can get the [Postgres `EXPLAIN` execution plan](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-explain.html) of a query\\\\nusing the `explain()` method. This works on any query, even for `rpc()` or writes.\\\\n\\\\nExplain is not enabled by default as it can reveal sensitive information about your database.\\\\nIt's best to only enable this for testing environments but if you wish to enable it for production you can provide additional protection by using a `pre-request` function.\\\\n\\\\nFollow the [Performance Debugging Guide](/docs/guides/database/debugging-performance) to enable the functionality on your project.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Examples\\\\n\\\\n### Get the execution plan\\\\n\\\\n```dart\\\\nfinal data = await supabase\\\\n .from('instruments')\\\\n .select()\\\\n .explain();\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Get the execution plan with analyze and verbose\\\\n\\\\n```dart\\\\nfinal data = await supabase\\\\n .from('instruments')\\\\n .select()\\\\n .explain(analyze:true, verbose:true);\\\\n```\\\\n\\\"},{\\\"title\\\":\\\"How Postgres chooses which index to use\\\",\\\"href\\\":\\\"https://supabase.com/docs/guides/troubleshooting/how-postgres-chooses-which-index-to-use-_JHrf4\\\",\\\"content\\\":\\\"# How Postgres chooses which index to use\\\\n\\\\n> For the curious: [here is a list of all built-in indexes in Postgres](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-types.html)\\\\n\\\\n### Postgres internals\\\\n\\\\n#### How an index is chosen\\\\n\\\\nPostgres, internally, contains a few components that manage query execution:\\\\n\\\\n| Module | Description |\\\\n| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |\\\\n| Parser | Converts SQL into an traversable query tree |\\\\n| Planner/Optimizer | Takes the query tree and uses rules and database statistics to find the optimal strategy for getting the data |\\\\n| Executor | Executes the plan created by the planner |\\\\n\\\\nThe planner will consider using an index when an indexed column is present in a filter statement, such as:\\\\n\\\\n* `WHERE`\\\\n* `LIKE`\\\\n* `ILIKE`\\\\n* `DISTINCT`\\\\n* `SIMILAR TO`\\\\n* `JOIN`\\\\n* `ORDER BY`\\\\n\\\\nOtherwise, it will likely perform a full table scan (sequential scan).\\\\n\\\\nIn the majority of cases, the indexed column must not only be present but also must be filtered by a comparison operator (`=`, `>`, `<>`) that is compatible with the index.\\\\n\\\\nAs an example, one can create the following table:\\\\n\\\\n| Column Name | Data Type |\\\\n| ----------- | --------- |\\\\n| id | INT |\\\\n| data | JSONB |\\\\n\\\\nOn the data column, a GIN index can be applied, which is excellent for filtering JSONB datatypes:\\\\n\\\\n```SQL\\\\nCREATE INDEX some_arbitary_index_name ON some_table USING gin (data);\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nHere's a [link](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/gist-builtin-opclasses.html) to the list operators supported by the GIN index; notably, it does not support greater than `>`:\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\n-- GIN index will never be used\\\\nselect *\\\\nfrom some_table\\\\nwhere data -> val > 5;\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nGIN does support the `@>` operator:\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\n--GIN will be considered\\\\nSELECT id FROM some_table\\\\nWHERE data @> '[ { \\\\\\\"itemId\\\\\\\": \\\\\\\"p11\\\\\\\" } ]';\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nIn most cases, developers work with the default BTREE index. It is the most practical and performant in the majority of cases and is compatible with the following filter [operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/btree-behavior.html):\\\\n\\\\n| Comparison Operator |\\\\n| ------------------- |\\\\n| `<` |\\\\n| `<=` |\\\\n| `=` |\\\\n| `>=` |\\\\n| `>` |\\\\n\\\\nAn operator's functional equivalents, such as `IN`, `BETWEEN`, and `ANY`, are also valid.\\\\n\\\\nHowever, just because the base requirements (relevant column, filter, and operators) are present, doesn't mean that an index will be used.\\\\n\\\\nIndexes have a startup cost, so for small tables, Postgres might use a sequential scan if it believes that it will take less time. The database keeps statistics about each table that it uses to inform these choices.\\\\n\\\\nIn very rare cases, these statistics can become stale, and Postgres may opt to use a slower index or sequential scan when a better option is available.\\\\n\\\\nYou can see the query plan with the `EXPLAIN` keyword:\\\\n\\\\n EXPLAIN \\\\n\\\\nTo understand how to interpret its output, you can check out this [explainer](https://github.com/orgs/supabase/discussions/22839).\\\\n\\\\nTo reset statistics within the database, you can use the following query:\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\n-- use judiciously\\\\nselect pg_stat_reset();\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n### Complex or composite indexes\\\\n\\\\n> For a more complete rundown, check the [Postgres Official Docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-multicolumn.html)\\\\n\\\\n#### Multi-column indexes\\\\n\\\\nIf you make independent indexes on multiple columns, Postgres will likely use each of them independently to find the relevant rows and then combine the results together.\\\\n\\\\nIt is possible to make [multi-column indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-multicolumn.html). If you are regularly filtering against multiple columns, there can be performance benefits using them instead of several independent indexes.\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\n-- multi-column index\\\\ncreate index test2_mm_idx on test2 (major, minor);\\\\n\\\\n-- multi-column comparison:\\\\nselect name\\\\nfrom test2\\\\nwhere major = constant and minor = constant;\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n#### Ordered indexes\\\\n\\\\nIf you're using an ORDER BY clause, [indexes can also be pre-sorted by DESC/ASC](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-ordering.html) for better performance.\\\\n\\\\n -- organizes the index in a DESC order, places NULL values at the end\\\\n CREATE INDEX test3_desc_index ON test3 (id DESC NULLS LAST);\\\\n\\\\n#### Functional indexes\\\\n\\\\nAlthough not as common, indexes can also be leveraged against modified values, such as when using a LOWER function:\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\n-- Index on modified column through function\\\\ncreate index test1_lower_col1_idx on test1 (lower(col1));\\\\n\\\\n-- Index will be considered for the following query:\\\\nselect * from test1 where lower(col1) = 'value';\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n#### Covering indexes\\\\n\\\\nIndexes contain pointers to a specific row, but you could instruct an index to actually hold a copy of a column's value for even faster retrieval. These are known as `covering` indexes. Because maintaining a copy is storage intensive, you should avoid using it for values with large data footprints.[ FULL VIDEO ON TOPIC](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bBu_V8CfWgM)\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\nCREATE INDEX a_b_idx ON x (a,b) INCLUDE (c);\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n#### Indexes on JSONB\\\\n\\\\nAlthough a GIN/GIST index can be used to index entire JSONB bodies, you can also target just specific Key-values with standard BTREE indexes:\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\n-- Example table\\\\ncreate table person (\\\\n id serial primary key,\\\\n data jsonb\\\\n);\\\\n\\\\ncreate index index_name on person ((data ->> 'name'));\\\\n```\\\\n\\\"},{\\\"title\\\":\\\"Full Text Search\\\",\\\"href\\\":\\\"https://supabase.com/docs/guides/database/full-text-search\\\",\\\"content\\\":\\\"# Full Text Search\\\\n\\\\nHow to use full text search in PostgreSQL.\\\\n\\\\nPostgres has built-in functions to handle `Full Text Search` queries. This is like a \\\\\\\"search engine\\\\\\\" within Postgres.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Preparation\\\\n\\\\nFor this guide we'll use the following example data:\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n \\\\n {/* supa-mdx-lint-disable Rule003Spelling */}\\\\n\\\\n | id | title | author | description |\\\\n | -- | ----------------------------------- | ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |\\\\n | 1 | The Poky Little Puppy | Janette Sebring Lowrey | Puppy is slower than other, bigger animals. |\\\\n | 2 | The Tale of Peter Rabbit | Beatrix Potter | Rabbit eats some vegetables. |\\\\n | 3 | Tootle | Gertrude Crampton | Little toy train has big dreams. |\\\\n | 4 | Green Eggs and Ham | Dr. Seuss | Sam has changing food preferences and eats unusually colored food. |\\\\n | 5 | Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire | J.K. Rowling | Fourth year of school starts, big drama ensues. |\\\\n\\\\n {/* supa-mdx-lint-enable Rule003Spelling */}\\\\n \\\\n\\\\n \\\\n ```sql\\\\n create table books (\\\\n id serial primary key,\\\\n title text,\\\\n author text,\\\\n description text\\\\n );\\\\n\\\\n insert into books\\\\n (title, author, description)\\\\n values\\\\n (\\\\n 'The Poky Little Puppy',\\\\n 'Janette Sebring Lowrey',\\\\n 'Puppy is slower than other, bigger animals.'\\\\n ),\\\\n ('The Tale of Peter Rabbit', 'Beatrix Potter', 'Rabbit eats some vegetables.'),\\\\n ('Tootle', 'Gertrude Crampton', 'Little toy train has big dreams.'),\\\\n (\\\\n 'Green Eggs and Ham',\\\\n 'Dr. Seuss',\\\\n 'Sam has changing food preferences and eats unusually colored food.'\\\\n ),\\\\n (\\\\n 'Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire',\\\\n 'J.K. Rowling',\\\\n 'Fourth year of school starts, big drama ensues.'\\\\n );\\\\n ```\\\\n \\\\n\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Usage\\\\n\\\\nThe functions we'll cover in this guide are:\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### `to_tsvector()` \\\\\\\\[#to-tsvector]\\\\n\\\\nConverts your data into searchable tokens. `to_tsvector()` stands for \\\\\\\"to text search vector.\\\\\\\" For example:\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\nselect to_tsvector('green eggs and ham');\\\\n-- Returns 'egg':2 'green':1 'ham':4\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nCollectively these tokens are called a \\\\\\\"document\\\\\\\" which Postgres can use for comparisons.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### `to_tsquery()` \\\\\\\\[#to-tsquery]\\\\n\\\\nConverts a query string into tokens to match. `to_tsquery()` stands for \\\\\\\"to text search query.\\\\\\\"\\\\n\\\\nThis conversion step is important because we will want to \\\\\\\"fuzzy match\\\\\\\" on keywords.\\\\nFor example if a user searches for `eggs`, and a column has the value `egg`, we probably still want to return a match.\\\\n\\\\nPostgres provides several functions to create tsquery objects:\\\\n\\\\n* **`to_tsquery()`** - Requires manual specification of operators (`&`, `|`, `!`)\\\\n* **`plainto_tsquery()`** - Converts plain text to an AND query: `plainto_tsquery('english', 'fat rats')` \\u2192 `'fat' & 'rat'`\\\\n* **`phraseto_tsquery()`** - Creates phrase queries: `phraseto_tsquery('english', 'fat rats')` \\u2192 `'fat' <-> 'rat'`\\\\n* **`websearch_to_tsquery()`** - Supports web search syntax with quotes, \\\\\\\"or\\\\\\\", and negation\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Match: `@@` \\\\\\\\[#match]\\\\n\\\\nThe `@@` symbol is the \\\\\\\"match\\\\\\\" symbol for Full Text Search. It returns any matches between a `to_tsvector` result and a `to_tsquery` result.\\\\n\\\\nTake the following example:\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n \\\\n ```sql\\\\n select *\\\\n from books\\\\n where title = 'Harry';\\\\n ```\\\\n \\\\n\\\\n \\\\n ```js\\\\n const { data, error } = await supabase.from('books').select().eq('title', 'Harry')\\\\n ```\\\\n \\\\n\\\\n \\\\n ```dart\\\\n final result = await client\\\\n .from('books')\\\\n .select()\\\\n .eq('title', 'Harry');\\\\n ```\\\\n \\\\n\\\\n \\\\n ```swift\\\\n let response = try await supabase.from(\\\\\\\"books\\\\\\\")\\\\n .select()\\\\n .eq(\\\\\\\"title\\\\\\\", value: \\\\\\\"Harry\\\\\\\")\\\\n .execute()\\\\n ```\\\\n \\\\n\\\\n \\\\n ```kotlin\\\\n val data = supabase.from(\\\\\\\"books\\\\\\\").select {\\\\n filter {\\\\n eq(\\\\\\\"title\\\\\\\", \\\\\\\"Harry\\\\\\\")\\\\n }\\\\n }\\\\n ```\\\\n \\\\n\\\\n \\\\n ```python\\\\n data = supabase.from_('books').select().eq('title', 'Harry').execute()\\\\n ```\\\\n \\\\n\\\\n\\\\nThe equality symbol above (`=`) is very \\\\\\\"strict\\\\\\\" on what it matches. In a full text search context, we might want to find all \\\\\\\"Harry Potter\\\\\\\" books and so we can rewrite the\\\\nexample above:\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n \\\\n ```sql\\\\n select *\\\\n from books\\\\n
